summary: This informational memo describes how sites connect to multiple providers with IPv4, which is essential for many Internet sites. It lists features useful for comparing with multihoming proposals, especially those related to IPv6.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv4 sites can connect to several providers in different ways, using BGP, multiple links to one provider or provider-assigned addresses with NAT. RFC 4116 describes the trade-offs so other multihoming proposals can be compared with current practice.

questions: how do sites connect to multiple isps
subtitle: How IPv4 sites connect to multiple providers and what the approaches require.

tldr.problem: Sites may want more than one path to the Internet, while IPv4 routing and address aggregation are organized around provider hierarchies.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes BGP announcements using provider-independent or provider-aggregatable addresses, multiple attachments to one provider, and NAT- or RFC 2260-based multihoming.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4116 records IPv4 practices and compares their features for evaluating other multihoming proposals. It is Informational and does not analyze their security implications.

today: RFC 4116 is an Informational memo published in July 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the memo does not analyze multihoming security.

sections.title: What Multihoming Means
sections.content:
A multihomed site connects to more than one transit provider. A transit provider gives the site connectivity beyond its own network and direct customers. A site with multiple layer-3 connections to one provider is called multi-attached.

IPv4 multihoming practices were added to the CIDR routing architecture, which aggregates routes according to provider and customer relationships. This memo records common practices and lists features that can be compared with other proposals, particularly proposals related to IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Multihoming connects a site to more than one transit provider so that it has more than one route to the Internet. Multi-attachment adds several connections to one provider.

sections.title: Provider-Independent and Provider-Aggregatable Addresses
sections.content:
Provider-Independent (PI) addresses are globally unique and are not assigned by a transit provider; they usually come from a Regional Internet Registry. Provider-Aggregatable (PA) addresses are assigned by a transit provider and are usually covered by that provider's aggregate route.

Using PI addresses with BGP makes the site's route visible across multiple providers, but each PI site adds a prefix to the global routing system. A site using PA addresses may need to renumber if it stops using the provider that assigned them.
sections.plainLanguage: PI addresses are assigned independently of a transit provider. PA addresses come from a provider, and a site may need to change them when it leaves that provider.

sections.title: BGP Multihoming
sections.content:
A site can announce routes to two or more transit providers using BGP, giving the Internet multiple paths back to the site. With PI addresses, each site contributes a route prefix. The memo notes that policies for PI assignments became less liberal than they were in the mid-1990s, when a /24 was generally accepted with little justification.

A site can also use PA addresses from one primary provider and ask additional providers to announce the site's routes. Other networks may filter these more-specific routes, increasing dependence on the primary provider. A site can use its own globally unique AS number for a consistent route origin, or use other origin arrangements with trade-offs for troubleshooting.
sections.plainLanguage: With BGP, a site announces its routes to multiple providers. PI addresses avoid dependence on one assigning provider, while PA addresses may be filtered or require renumbering when the primary provider changes.

sections.title: Multi-Attachment and NAT-Based Options
sections.content:
Multiple connections to one transit provider can add redundancy without adding global routing state. BGP is not required, but some method must reroute traffic after a failure. This approach does not protect the site against failure of the provider itself.

In NAT- or RFC 2260-based multihoming, a site uses PA addresses from each provider. Hosts may use those addresses directly, or NAT may translate them to private-use addresses. Providers need not make special arrangements, and the method adds no global routing state, but it generally does not preserve transport-layer sessions during a re-homing event.
sections.plainLanguage: Several links to one provider avoid extra global routes but do not protect against that provider failing. NAT-based options can avoid global route growth, but transport sessions usually do not survive a change of provider.

sections.title: Comparing the Trade-Offs
sections.content:
The memo compares redundancy, load sharing, performance, policy, simplicity, transport-layer survivability, DNS, packet filtering, scalability, router and host impact, and provider cooperation. All the described approaches provide some redundancy and load sharing, but the methods differ in how they steer inbound and outbound traffic.

BGP-based methods can provide some transport-session survivability, although long route convergence can cause sessions to time out. RFC 2260/NAT multihoming generally does not preserve sessions through re-homing. The memo says BGP-based practices add global routing state, while NAT-based multihoming and multi-attachment to one provider do not.
sections.plainLanguage: The methods differ in route growth, provider independence, traffic control and session continuity. The memo compares these features rather than declaring one approach best for every site.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content: RFC 4116 describes IPv4 multihoming practices but does not analyze their security implications. It is an Informational snapshot intended to support comparisons with other multihoming approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: The document records IPv4 multihoming practices and trade-offs. It does not provide a security analysis or define a new multihoming protocol.
